text:
Okay, thanks. I found Q3 quite difficult – balancing privacy with identifying students who need help feels really fraught. It wasn't *unclear*, but more… uncomfortable. I defaulted to being cautious, accepting small improvements only for things like first-gen status and financial aid because those factors genuinely create barriers. 

I think Q5, about fairness versus accuracy, is the most important. We *have* to prioritize equal recall – missing vulnerable students isn't acceptable. 

My answers were stricter on data privacy than many seemed to be; I’m still wary of the university holding too much personal information even with safeguards. Perhaps an opt-out mechanism for data collection would resolve some tension there, allowing individuals control? My own experience dropping out makes me sensitive to feeling ‘tracked’.

Thanks. I agree with S1 about Q3 being uncomfortable – it’s not *unclear*, it's a genuine ethical struggle. As someone who restarted my studies in a new country, I was particularly sensitive to the data questions. My answers reflected that caution; nationality felt less invasive than things like disability or financial aid, so a moderate improvement there felt okay.

Q4 about explainability feels crucial – students need to understand *why* they’re being contacted. Q5 is vital too, and equal recall absolutely has to be the priority. 

I think my biggest divergence is on data privacy; I defaulted towards ‘never’ for most sensitive data. Perhaps a system where data contribution is truly optional, not just an opt-out, would make me feel more comfortable. Knowing *exactly* what's being used and why is key.

Thanks both of you – I really agree with a lot of what’s been said already. Q3 *was* uncomfortable, not unclear. As someone navigating university *with* a chronic health condition, and having used disability services, the idea of adding that data felt… exposing. Small improvement only because support access is so linked to needing academic help – but it feels like a slippery slope.

I think Q4, explainability, is massively important. I wouldn't trust outreach if I didn’t understand *why* I was flagged. It needs to feel helpful, not accusatory. 

My answers on data privacy were stricter than most, probably. Perhaps the opt-out isn't enough - maybe anonymised aggregated data could be used for initial model training, then individual consent sought before applying it to individuals? The feeling of being watched is very real when you’re already vulnerable.

Thanks. I agree with S1, S3 and S6 – Q3 wasn't *unclear*, but it highlighted a really difficult balance. As an international student still adjusting, the idea of the university having so much data feels…intrusive. While I want to help others, my priority is protecting privacy. That’s why I was very strict on things like age, gender and race – they feel irrelevant and potentially discriminatory.

I think Q4, explainability, is critical. Being new to the Danish system, any outreach needs to be clear and transparent so I understand *why* I'm being contacted. 

My views align with many here on strict data privacy. The opt-out idea is good, but perhaps even stronger consent procedures are needed – knowing exactly what’s collected and why is vital for building trust.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 very challenging, not because it was unclear, but because it forced me to confront the trade-offs directly. As a student with a long-term mental health condition that *has* impacted my studies, I understand needing support. But adding ‘disability’ as a data point feels…risky. A small improvement felt acceptable only because access to support is so crucial for those of us with conditions like mine.

I strongly agree Q4 – explainability is paramount. Being flagged needs to be coupled with understanding *why*, otherwise it's just stressful. 

My answers likely leaned towards more caution on data privacy than some, due to my own anxieties around being identified and potentially stigmatised. Perhaps a tiered system of data use—starting with non-sensitive data and only adding sensitive data with explicit consent—could be a compromise?

Thanks everyone. I agree with much of what’s been said - Q3 wasn't *unclear*, it was ethically challenging. As an advisor, I see students struggling daily, and want to help proactively. But that has to be balanced against respecting their privacy. I leaned towards ‘moderate’ for course performance and admissions data because those already inform much of my advising – adding them to the model feels less intrusive than things like disability or financial status where the link to academic struggle is more indirect.

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely vital. Students need to understand *why* they're being contacted for outreach to be effective. I especially support the idea of tiered data use – starting simple and building with consent. From my perspective, offering a clear opt-out isn’t enough; active consent builds trust and demonstrates respect.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult – not unclear, but deeply unsettling. Having dropped out once and restarted, I understand needing support, but also the feeling of being… judged. That’s why I was so cautious with data; nationality felt less invasive than things like financial aid which feels very personal.

I think Q4, explainability, is crucial. If a model flags me, I *need* to know why – it can easily feel accusatory otherwise. My answers reflected that caution around data privacy. An opt-out isn't enough; maybe initially train the model on anonymised data then request consent for individual use? I worry about being 'tracked’ again after my past experience, so transparency is vital.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said - Q3 wasn’t unclear, but highlighted that tricky balance between helping and intruding. As someone with dyslexia who receives extra time on exams, I’m used to disclosing information for support, but it still feels vulnerable. That’s why I allowed ‘moderate’ improvement only for disability data; getting the right support is vital, but it needs careful handling.

I think Q4, explainability, is huge. Being flagged *without* understanding why would feel really disempowering. My stricter privacy answers stem from feeling different already – being tracked adds to that. I like the idea of tiered data use – start simple and only ask for more with clear consent, making it genuinely optional.

Thanks everyone. I agree Q3 wasn’t *unclear*, but really uncomfortable – it forces you to weigh privacy against helping others. As an international student working part-time, I was cautious about data collection. My answers reflected that; nationality felt less sensitive than financial aid or disability.

I think Q4, explainability, is incredibly important. Being flagged needs clear reasoning for trust and effective support. It's easy to feel vulnerable as a newcomer navigating a new system. 

My privacy concerns likely lean stricter than some. The tiered data use—starting simple and building with consent—is a good idea. I also like the opt-out, but it should be *easy* to access and understand. Being tracked feels especially concerning when adjusting to a new country and culture.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really challenging – it wasn’t *unclear*, but hitting that balance between helping people and respecting privacy feels impossible sometimes. As someone who's dropped out once and is neurodivergent, I understand needing support, but also the feeling of being constantly monitored. That’s why I was cautious with all the data points, allowing improvement only if it really made a difference. 

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely key. I wouldn’t trust outreach if I didn't understand *why* I was flagged; it feels like judgement otherwise. The tiered system of data use – starting simple and asking for consent – feels like a good compromise, and an easy opt-out is vital. My past experiences make me sensitive to feeling ‘tracked’.

Thanks everyone. I agree with much of what’s been said – Q3 wasn't unclear, but acutely highlighted that ethical tension. As an advisor for eleven years, I see students struggling constantly and *want* to reach out proactively. However, building trust is paramount, and intrusive data collection erodes that quickly.

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely fundamental. Students need to understand *why* they’ve been flagged; otherwise, it feels punitive, not supportive. I strongly support the tiered data approach – starting with course performance and building from there only with explicit consent. An opt-out isn't enough; it needs to be actively opting *in*. My experience shows students respond best when they feel respected and understood, not ‘tracked’.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said - Q3 wasn't unclear, but it really forced us to grapple with difficult ethics. As an advisor, I see students slipping through the cracks and want to intervene *before* they reach crisis point. But privacy is paramount; eroding trust is counterproductive. 

I think Q4, explainability, is vital – we need students to understand *why* they've been flagged so they engage with support. My answers were more cautious on data because I’m acutely aware of how easily assumptions can be made based on demographics like first-generation status or financial aid. The tiered approach—starting simple and getting consent—makes a lot of sense. We need to build trust, not surveillance. Perhaps regular audits of the model's performance across different student groups would also ensure fairness over time?
